newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan stocks discount Deng's death, uptrend seen.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan stocks discount Deng's death, uptrend seen.

text.p: Taiwan share prices shrugged off the death of Chinese paramount leader Deng Xiaoping to close higher on Thursday, and analysts expected the market to continue seeking new highs while ignoring post-Deng political concerns.
Buoyed by widespread hope that Taiwan's economy would launch a sharp recovery in 1997, the stock market may soar past the 8,000-point level by the end of March, analysts predicted.
"Today's session made it very clear that the market's bull run has created a momentum that could not be stopped -- even by Deng," said Allen Huang, a fund manager for National Securities.
"This market could very well hit 8,000 by the end of March," Huang said.
On Thursday the weighted index recovered from an early fall to close 21.19 points or 0.28 percent higher at 7,678.04.
Turnover was a frantic T$153.19 billion (US$5.6 billion).
The market has finished higher in 12 of its last 14 sessions, gaining more than 500 points during that span and notching its highest levels in six years.

Rumours of Deng's failing health first hit the market on Tuesday and caused a mild sell-off during that session. But brokers said investors no longer feared that political chaos would emerge in China following the patriarch's death.

"(China's President) Jiang Zemin pretty much has solidified his power base, at least for the short term, so investors are not worried about any instability that might affect Taiwan," said David Yu, vice president of International Investment Trust Co.
The island's biggest investor in China, business conglomerate President Enterprises, said on Thursday it had no plans to curtail its huge US$900 million investment on the mainland.

President's chief executive officer Kao Ching-yuan, who in 1996 led a large business delegation to Beijing and met with Jiang, said most Taiwanese investors had already factored Deng's death into their investment plans.
"Deng's death was something all businessmen were expecting, so there is no reason for them to be nervous," said Kao, who doubles as chairman of the Chinese National Federation of Industries.

Analysts said Deng's death may actually create a bullish factor by dissuading Taiwan's government from trying to curb the market's recent sharp growth out of concern that such measures might cause the index to drop during this politically sensitive time.

"Before Deng's death the central bank had hinted that it may want to slow down the market's growth. Now there is no way the central bank would do such a thing," said George Hou, a fund manager for Jardine Fleming.

Central bank governor Sheu Yuan-dong said recently that Taiwan's stock market had "risen slightly too much". But on Thursday the government pledged to use measures to stabilise the market if it began to plunge after Deng's death.
Brokers said they observed moderate government-backed buying during Thursday's session, but for the most part the market carried itself.
